candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

The caption provides visual information about a document focused on electrical characteristics, which aligns with the technical topics discussed in the comment.
candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.

candidates.comment: This video began by introducing a previous video titled, “BJTs and Transistor Switches.” So for context I decided to back and watch this video first.   From this I was able to gain a baseline understanding of BJTs as electronic switches to determine how they differ from MOSFETS. BJTs are well suited for applications with small currents (less than one amp), whereas MOSFETS are suitable for applications with much higher currents. BJT stands for Bipolar Junction Transistor. The BJT has 3 terminals, the emitter, base, and collector. The transistor is made up of two diodes, one between base and emitter, and one between base and collector. Diodes need these current limits to work correctly. The two primary capabilities of the BJT are to amplify current, and secondly to operate as an electronic switch. There are 2 types of BJTs the NPN and the PNP. The NPN contains a forward-facing diode between bases and emitter, whereas the PNP contains a backward facing one. Both types will behave differently. MOSFET stands for Metal-Oxide Semiconductor Field Effect Transistor. MOSFETS are typically suited for applications with higher currents. They have two types of modes, depletion, and enhancement. Depletion mode works like a ‘normally closed’ switch, current can flow when no voltage is applied. Applied voltage (negative) causes the “switch” to open and stop the current. Enhancement mode MOSFETs work more like a variable resistor than an on and off switch. They come in N and P types. They are the most commonly used type of MOSFET. MOSFETs have a gate, drain, and source. The field effect nature suggests they work by voltage, compared to BJT that works by current. Voltage is applied be and source in varying intensities, which allows current to flow between the drain and source in varying intensities. Thus, they act as voltage dependent variable resistors. Increased voltage corresponds to lower resistance and higher current flow. Since MOSFETs are often used in high current applications they do have a tendency to get hot and can possibly require a heat sink. The maximum dissipation for safe operation without a heat sink can be simply calculated.  Threshold voltage is important for this calculation.
